answer.exemplar: A dated lending record has what a statement of grievance lacks: each entry carries a date, a sum, a rate asked and a note of whether the loan was taken, so the order of events can be checked and the month in which a government lost its freedom of action can be identified. A grievance states a reason, and reasons have no timestamp: the same complaint can be found in pamphlets written before the change, which is what makes it useless for dating and easy to use afterwards as an account of why the change was justified. That is why the money record usually appears first in the chronology. A strong answer also marks the limit of its own conclusion, since dating a fiscal pressure shows when the government was forced to act, and does not show that the grievances were unreal or that the pressure was the only cause worth considering.

answer.exemplar: The settlement is designed to be stable in the two places where instability would begin. A penalty confined to persons and offices removes the men who could coordinate a claim, and a list of names ages: as those men die, the organisation that could revive a grievance has no one left to lead it. At the same time, confirming the holdings leaves the winners with a reason to keep the text exactly as it stands, since any new disturbance is a threat to what they now own, and it gives the defeated a settlement in which their own property is safe, which is the most they can be offered by anyone. The result is a peace held by interest rather than by affection, and the weak answer is the one that calls it a compromise between honourable men, since nothing in the text depends on anyone's honour. A strong answer also names the condition of its own survival, which is that the property question stays closed.

questions.explanation: This is an explanatory item, so credit goes to a response that identifies where a settlement's stability comes from - the ageing of an excluded leadership and the alignment of both sides' interests in the confirmed holdings. The characteristic weak answer explains durability in terms of the moderation or honour of the men who made it, which is a disposition rather than a mechanism, and a second common error treats the punishment as the source of stability when it is the restriction of its organisation that does the work.

answer.exemplar: A language can be installed and used without being believed, which is the whole difference. Once the schools, the courts and the offices all work in one printed form, a man in any town is taught, judged and dealt with by the state in the same medium, and a text in that medium reaches him whether or not he feels any affection for the people who print it; the machinery of the state therefore does the work of persuasion, and a subject who has never met a fellow national can still be addressed, taxed and mobilised as one. A claim of common descent asks the opposite of him: it requires that he accept a story about a past he did not witness and feel a kinship toward strangers, and no officer or school can make him do either. A strong answer also states the price, because a standard imposed by a state is a claim that is still being asserted, and the same medium that unites also gives anyone who rejects it a ready means of organised complaint.

questions.explanation: This is an explanatory item, so credit goes to a response that identifies the mechanism - a medium the state can require and a reader can use without believing - rather than to one that says a shared language is more natural or more powerful. The characteristic weak answer treats a descent claim as merely false rather than as a claim of a kind that cannot be enforced, and a second common error stops at the successes of standardisation without noticing that the same institution is what a later dissenter will organise against.
